concept.name: Swing trading
concept.definition: A speculative trading style in which positions are held for one or more days up to several weeks to profit from short- to medium-term price 'swings'. Holding periods sit between day trading (closed intraday) and position trading or buy-and-hold (months to years), and entries/exits are typically driven by technical analysis, sometimes combined with fundamentals.
concept.intuition: The swing trader tries to catch the middle chunk of a move that plays out over days, without needing to buy the exact bottom or sell the exact top.
concept.mechanics: Traders identify setups (trend continuation, pullbacks to support, breakouts) on daily or intraday charts, enter with predefined stops and targets, and hold overnight, accepting gap risk in exchange for capturing multi-day moves. Rule-based swing systems encode entry/exit as objective technical rules.
concept.failure_modes: Overnight and weekend gaps can blow through stops; in choppy, trendless markets swing signals whipsaw and repeated small losses accumulate.
concept.misconceptions: That swing trading reliably times tops and bottoms, or that widely followed rule-based setups keep their edge; competition and regime change erode simple swing rules.
concept.example: A trader buys a stock pulling back to its rising 20-day average at $88, places a stop at $85 and a target at $96, and exits eight trading days later.
